title: US AI rally lifts Asian markets as Indian indices brace for holiday close
excerpt: Wall Street surged on the Nvidia AI bounce, pulling the FTSE 100 higher and sparking a rally in Japan and Hong Kong. Indian markets opened lower on the back of a weaker risk tone, with the rupee flat at 92.90 and volatility edging up.

What happened

India

The Nifty 50 closed at 25,349.65 rupees, down 1.75% on Monday, while the Sensex slipped 1.77% to 82,435.99. The banking gauge bore the brunt, falling 3.17% to 62,585.35, whereas the IT index bucked the trend, rising 1.69% to 31,850.80. The India VIX rose 2.18% to 17.70, signalling a modest uptick in market nervousness. Across the broader NSE, financials fell 2.31%, PSU banks dropped 3.25%, autos slipped 1.03%, pharma eased 0.35%, FMCG declined 0.46%, metals plunged 3.68%, energy slipped 1.78% and realty edged up 0.31%. The mixed performance reflects a tug‑of‑war between global AI optimism and lingering risk aversion.

Sector breadth was uneven. IT stocks led the rally, supported by domestic demand for software services and a spill‑over from the AI‑driven Nasdaq surge. Real estate managed a modest gain, hinting at some investor confidence in property assets. In contrast, banks and metal stocks suffered the steepest declines, mirroring concerns over higher US yields and a potential slowdown in credit growth. The energy sector’s 1.78% fall aligns with the dip in Brent crude, while consumer‑oriented FMCG and pharma showed only marginal weakness, suggesting that defensive plays remain in demand despite the broader sell‑off.

The rupee held steady at 92.90 per dollar, unchanged in live trading, indicating that the currency’s recent carry‑trade appeal has not yet eroded despite a stronger dollar environment. Analysts note that the RBI’s temporary policy stance has turned the rupee into an accidental carry star, but the advantage has narrowed since 2011. With oil prices easing and foreign inflows shifting from AI‑heavy equities to Indian markets, the rupee’s stability may be short‑lived if US rate expectations intensify or global risk sentiment turns more bearish.

Indian markets are closed today for Guru Nanak Jayanti, with the BSE and NSE observing a holiday. MCX will pause morning trading and resume in the evening session, while NCDEX remains shut for the day. Traders will look ahead to the next trading session for clues on how the AI‑fuelled rally in the US and Asia will translate into domestic momentum, especially as the Nifty and Bank Nifty are expected to open lower if risk aversion persists. Key data releases later this week, including domestic inflation and RBI policy commentary, will be closely watched.

Global markets

Wall Street rebounded sharply on Monday, with the S&P 500 up 4.73% to 7,237.17, the Nasdaq climbing 6.51% to 24,089.56 and the Dow Jones gaining 3.01% to 49,595.31. The surge was anchored by Nvidia’s 31.5% jump after the board reinstated Jensen Huang, reviving AI‑related buying. Treasury yields rose, pushing the US 10‑year to 4.92%, while the dollar firmed, creating a mixed backdrop for emerging markets that must balance higher funding costs against renewed equity enthusiasm.

European equities followed the US lead, with the FTSE 100 rising 1.30% to 10,480.82 on Monday. The modest gain reflected improved risk sentiment as investors digested the AI rally and the prospect of continued corporate earnings growth. However, European markets remain cautious about the trajectory of US monetary policy, and any further yield hikes could temper the optimism that has lifted the continent’s blue‑chip indices.

In Asia, the Nikkei 225 is up 3.85% in early trade, trading at 58,607.70, while Hong Kong’s Hang Seng edged higher 0.25% to 22,440.58. The AI trade resurgence is spilling over, with Korean and Taiwanese benchmarks posting double‑digit gains in recent sessions. The live Asian momentum suggests that the AI‑driven risk appetite is still alive, but the impact on India will be muted today due to the holiday, though the sentiment may carry into the next trading day.

Rupee, rates and commodities

The rupee remained flat at 92.90 per dollar, indicating a brief pause in its recent strengthening despite a firmer US dollar. Lower oil prices, with Brent crude at $86.38, have eased import‑bill pressures, supporting the rupee’s stance. Commentary on the rupee’s accidental carry‑star status highlights that the RBI’s temporary incentives may not be sustainable, leaving the currency vulnerable to shifts in global risk sentiment and US monetary policy.

US Treasury yields climbed to 4.92% on Monday, up 0.12% from the previous close, reflecting market expectations of a tighter monetary stance. Higher yields typically raise the cost of capital for Indian corporates and can attract foreign investors away from emerging‑market equities, adding to the pressure on the Nifty and Bank Nifty. The modest rise in yields also underpins the dollar’s resilience, which has limited further rupee appreciation.

Commodities showed mixed signals: Brent crude slipped 0.35% to $86.38, providing some relief to the Indian balance of payments, while gold inched up 0.07% to $3,653.80, maintaining its safe‑haven appeal amid global volatility. Bitcoin fell 1.06% to $60,562.62, underscoring the broader risk‑off tone in crypto markets. These price movements, combined with today’s holiday in India, mean that market participants will watch upcoming US inflation data and RBI commentary for clues on the direction of yields, the rupee and Indian equity valuations.

News that matters

  1. Asian markets follow Wall Street: Nikkei, Kospi jump up to 8% as Jensen Huang’s return sparks rally in AI stocks

    Mint

    Asian markets rallied on Tuesday after Nvidia’s 31.5% surge on Wall Street revived confidence in AI‑related shares. The Nikkei climbed 4.5%, the KOSPI rose 7.5% and Taiwan’s benchmark jumped 9.1%, reflecting a broad AI‑driven bounce. For Indian investors, the rally lifted the Nifty IT index 1.69% to 31,850.80, while the broader Nifty 50 slipped 1.75% to 25,349.65, indicating that the AI tailwind was not enough to offset weakness elsewhere. The surge also fed into the rupee’s carry appeal, but the USD/INR held at 92.90, showing no immediate currency impact. The rally’s sustainability hinges on whether Nvidia can sustain its earnings momentum and whether US rate expectations remain stable; a reversal in US Treasury yields or a pull‑back in AI spending could quickly erode the gains across Asian equities, including India’s tech‑heavy exposure.

  2. India’s rupee has become an accidental carry star

    Economic Times

    The Economic Times reports that the rupee has become an accidental carry star after the RBI’s temporary measures attracted carry traders. The narrative cites falling oil prices and a shift of foreign capital from AI stocks to Indian markets as catalysts. The USD/INR is live at 92.90, unchanged from the previous close, suggesting that the rupee’s strength is holding for now. However, the article warns that RBI incentives may not be permanent and the interest‑rate advantage the rupee once enjoyed has eroded since 2011. For investors, the key risk is a sudden policy shift that could reverse the rupee’s carry appeal, prompting capital outflows and pressure on the currency. Any unexpected rise in US yields or a rebound in oil prices would also weigh on the rupee. Monitoring RBI statements and global yield curves will be essential to gauge whether the rupee’s carry status can be sustained or if it will revert to a more volatile trajectory.

  3. AI trade resurgence drives broad rally across Asian markets

    Moneycontrol.com

    Moneycontrol’s coverage notes that the AI trade resurgence sparked a broad rally across Asian markets, with the KOSPI up 7.5%, Taiwan’s index up 9.1% and Japan’s Nikkei gaining 4.5%. The rally was anchored by Nvidia’s 31.5% jump on Wall Street, which revived investor appetite for semiconductor and AI‑related stocks. In India, the Nifty IT index rose 1.69% to 31,850.80, but the broader Nifty 50 fell 1.75% to 25,349.65, indicating that the AI boost was sector‑specific. Export‑oriented sectors such as metals, down 3.68% to 11,819.25, may benefit from higher global demand if the AI‑driven growth sustains. Conversely, the rally could be fragile; any negative US data or a reversal in AI sentiment could pull Asian indices back, pressuring Indian equities further. Investors should watch US Treasury yields, which closed at 4.92%, and any policy signals from the Fed, as higher yields could dampen risk appetite and reverse the current AI‑fuelled optimism.

  4. Wall Street soars on Huang's return to Nvidia, Treasury yields rise

    Economic Times

    The Economic Times reports that US equities rebounded sharply on Monday after Nvidia reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO, lifting the Nasdaq 100 by 6.5% and the S&P 500 by 4.7%. Nvidia itself jumped 31%, driving the Nasdaq to close at 24,089.56 and the S&P at 7,237.17. Treasury yields rose 0.12% to 4.92%, and the dollar strengthened, pressuring the rupee, which remained flat at 92.90. In India, the Nifty 50 fell 1.75% to 25,349.65 and the Nifty Bank slipped 3.17% to 62,585.35, reflecting sensitivity to higher US yields and a stronger dollar. The rally’s upside is limited by the lingering risk of further yield hikes; any additional increase in US rates could deepen the pressure on Indian equities and the rupee. Investors should monitor upcoming US inflation data and Fed commentary, as well as domestic corporate earnings, to gauge whether the US market bounce can translate into sustained support for Indian risk assets.

  5. Teamsters urge US lawmakers to quickly pass Chinese car ban

    Reuters

    Reuters notes that the Teamsters are urging US lawmakers to pass a ban on Chinese cars quickly. If enacted, the ban would restrict imports of Chinese‑manufactured vehicles into the United States, potentially shifting demand toward domestic and alternative foreign producers. For Indian investors, the auto sector closed down 1.03% to 28,490.70, reflecting broader market weakness but also exposing the sector to any policy‑driven demand shifts. A US ban could open export opportunities for Indian auto manufacturers if they can capture displaced market share, but it also raises the risk of retaliatory trade measures that could affect Indian exports. The impact will depend on the speed and scope of the legislation, as well as the ability of Indian firms to meet US regulatory standards. Investors should watch US congressional activity and any early‑stage trade negotiations, as well as domestic auto earnings, to assess whether the policy change will translate into a material upside for Indian auto stocks.

  6. Stock market open today or not? BSE, NSE closed on 24 Nov for Guru Nanak Jayanti? Check holiday calendar

    Mint

    Mint confirms that Indian equity markets will be closed on 24 November for Guru Nanak Jayanti, with the BSE and NSE not trading. MCX will pause morning trading and resume from 5 pm to 11:30 pm, while NCDEX remains closed all day. The holiday removes a day of liquidity, compressing trading volume into the preceding and following sessions. Market participants will need to adjust risk management ahead of the break, especially given the volatile backdrop of US AI‑driven rallies and higher Treasury yields. Key data releases scheduled for today include US inflation figures and corporate earnings, which could set the tone for the next trading day. The absence of Indian market activity means that any sharp moves in global indices—such as the live Nikkei up 3.85% and Hang Seng up 0.25%—will be reflected in the opening levels on 25 November rather than being absorbed intraday.

Our view

cautious Analyst board aligned (3 of 3 views)

Wall Street closed on a high note on Monday, with the S&P 500 posting a 4.73% gain, the Nasdaq surging 6.51% and the Dow Jones climbing 3.01% versus the previous close. Across the Atlantic, the FTSE 100 added 1.30%. In Asia, the Nikkei 225 is live and up 3.85% while Hong Kong’s Hang Seng is modestly higher at 0.25%. The rally is being driven by a renewed AI narrative after Jensen Huang’s return to Nvidia, which has lifted risk‑appetite globally. However, the upside has yet to filter into Indian equities, suggesting a disconnect between global sentiment and domestic positioning.

India’s equity markets ended the last session sharply lower. The Nifty 50 fell 1.75% to 25,349.65, the Sensex slipped 1.77% to 82,435.99 and the Nifty Bank dropped a steeper 3.17% to 62,585.35. The India VIX rose 2.18% to 17.70, signalling heightened volatility. All major sector indices were in the red, with financials, metals and energy each down around 2‑4%. The market is closed today for Guru Nanak Jayanti, leaving the next trading day without a domestic catalyst and reinforcing the board’s cautious tone.

On the macro front, the rupee is flat at 92.90 per dollar, offering no currency‑driven support for exporters. The US 10‑year Treasury yield edged higher to 4.92%, a level that can pressure equity valuations. Brent crude slipped 0.35% to $86.38, limiting upside for energy‑linked stocks, while gold ticked up to $3,653.80, reflecting a modest safe‑haven demand. With limited external tailwinds and a volatile domestic backdrop, the risk‑adjusted case for aggressive positioning remains weak.

Given the sharp domestic sell‑off, elevated VIX, and the absence of a near‑term catalyst, the house stance stays cautious. The momentum strategist flags weak breadth despite the global rally, the risk manager highlights sector‑specific profit‑taking, and the macro economist points to a stagnant rupee and rising US yields as headwinds. Until fresh data or a clear shift in sentiment emerges, a defensive posture is warranted.

Sector calls

SectorCallWhy
FinancialsunderweightThe Financials index fell 2.31% on Monday, lagging the broader market, and the PSU Bank sub‑index dropped 3.25%. With banks under pressure from higher funding costs and a flat rupee, earnings momentum looks constrained, justifying a defensive tilt.
PSU BankunderweightPSU banks posted the steepest decline at 3.25%, reflecting heightened sensitivity to policy‑rate expectations and weaker loan growth. The sector’s risk‑return profile is unattractive until the funding environment eases.
AutoneutralThe Auto index slipped 1.03%, a modest pullback that mirrors broader market weakness rather than sector‑specific fundamentals. With demand data pending, a neutral stance allows flexibility for any near‑term catalyst.
PharmaneutralPharma edged down 0.35%, indicating relative resilience amid the sell‑off. The sector’s defensive nature and stable demand for healthcare products support a neutral positioning pending earnings updates.
FMCGneutralFMCG fell 0.46%, a marginal decline that suggests the sector is holding its ground despite broader risk aversion. Consumption trends remain steady, warranting a neutral view until consumer sentiment data arrives.
MetalunderweightMetal indices plunged 3.68%, driven by weaker global commodity prices and a modest dip in Brent crude. The sector faces headwinds from subdued demand and price pressure, supporting an underweight bias.
EnergyneutralEnergy slipped 1.78% as Brent fell 0.35%. While price weakness limits upside, the sector’s exposure to global demand recovery keeps it from a bearish stance, meriting neutrality.

What would change our view

If the US equity rally sustains into the week and foreign institutional inflows resume, Indian indices could catch up, eroding the current downside bias. A breakout above the recent lows would also lower the VIX, reducing volatility concerns.

A depreciation of the rupee below 92.90 or a pull‑back in US 10‑year yields could improve export competitiveness and lower financing costs, providing a tailwind for financials and metal stocks and challenging the cautious outlook.

Stronger-than‑expected domestic data—such as a surprise uptick in PMI, lower inflation, or robust corporate earnings—could revive risk appetite and trigger a bounce in the Nifty and Bank Nifty, undermining the underweight calls.

How the analyst board voted
  • Momentum strategist: cautious, conviction 3/5. Indian indices closed sharply lower (Nifty -1.75%, Bank Nifty -3.17%) with most sectors down and India VIX up 2.18%, signalling weak breadth and heightened risk aversion. US markets posted a strong rally (+4‑6% across S&P, Nasdaq, Dow) and Asian AI‑driven gains (Nikkei +3.85%) provide external upside, but the rally has not yet translated into Indian equity buying, especially in financials. USD/INR is flat at 92.90 and the market is closed today for Guru Nanak Jayanti, leaving the next session without a domestic catalyst; caution is warranted until fresh data or sentiment shifts.
  • Risk manager: cautious, conviction 4/5. Nifty and Sensex fell ~1.8% and Bank Nifty slid 3% despite a strong US rally (+4‑6%), signalling sector‑specific weakness and profit‑taking risk. India VIX rose 2.18% to 17.70, pointing to heightened volatility ahead of the post‑holiday open. Financials, metals and energy indices are all down 1%, while USD/INR is flat at 92.90 and Brent crude is only marginally lower, offering limited macro support.
  • Macro economist: cautious, conviction 3/5. US equities surged (+4.7% to +6.5%) and Asian AI‑driven rallies (Nikkei +3.9%) lifted global risk appetite, yet Indian indices opened lower (Nifty -1.75%, Bank Nifty -3.17%) with the India VIX up 2.2%, signalling heightened volatility. The rupee is stuck at 92.90 INR per USD despite a modest rise in US 10‑year yields (4.92%), limiting any currency‑driven tailwinds for export‑oriented stocks. Key domestic sectors are under pressure: Financials and PSU banks down 2%, metals down 3.7%, while commodities such as Brent crude slipped, dampening sentiment for commodity‑linked equities.

What to watch

  • US 10‑year Treasury yield movement for clues on global risk pricing.
  • Continuation of the AI‑driven rally in Asian markets, especially the Nikkei’s performance.
  • Brent crude price trajectory as a proxy for metal and energy sector health.
  • Upcoming Indian macro data releases, including inflation and PMI figures.
  • Any policy statements from the RBI regarding interest rates or liquidity.
